The only question is therefore this:
Can reflective empiricism actually explain the undeniable fact that science produces hypotheses of ever greater probability?
To answer this question, we need to go back to the origins of empiricism itself.

We have seen that sensory experience does not guarantee the existence of an objective reality independent of thought or discourse. After all, sensory experience can be entirely subjective and illusory, as it is in dreams.

Empiricism nevertheless had to introduce the idea of objective reality because the development of rationalism had shown that reason cannot produce any diversity by itself. Reason, or discourse, supplies only a unifying form. The diversity of its content has to come from outside, through sensory experience—from precisely what empiricism calls “reality.”

In other words, reason contributes the principle of unity: it identifies and brings together diverse contents. By contrast, the presence of “reality” can be recognized only through diversity and difference.

But if this is so, then the central idea of reflective empiricism—the idea of an “infinite progress” in which we produce increasingly plausible hypotheses—is impossible in principle. Indeed, the idea is internally contradictory.

A “plausible” hypothesis has to satisfy two demands at once. It must meet the basic demand of rationalism by being perfectly coherent and free of contradiction. And it must meet the basic demand of empiricism by corresponding to reality.

But the pursuit of coherence is a pursuit of greater unity, whereas getting closer to reality means moving toward ever greater multiplicity. If diversity is our only guarantee that we are dealing with reality, then empiricism is quite right to say that the most plausible—the most “true,” the closest to reality—hypothesis is the one capable of accounting for the greatest diversity of sensory experience.
Yet the more it does this, the further it moves from the rationalist demand for unity.

Conversely, suppose we call a hypothesis more “plausible,” more satisfying to reason, or more “elegant” when it is internally simple. Its sensory basis will then be extremely narrow, which makes it empirically much less plausible.

So if empiricism is right, this supposed “infinite progress” of science is impossible. All hypotheses will ultimately be equal in plausibility or implausibility. As they gain in elegance and unity, they lose in breadth; as they gain in breadth, they lose in unity. Choosing one over another then becomes a matter of personal taste. Progress itself becomes an illusion, because whatever a hypothesis gains on one side it loses on the other.
It is therefore hardly surprising that reflective empiricism was answered by a new—and final—form of empirical scepticism, which we can call positivism.
Like every form of scepticism, positivism decisively abandons the idea of truth, and especially the empirical definition of truth as a correspondence between discourse and reality.

Hypotheses are no longer described as “plausible.” They become merely useful or workable. They do not reveal an objective reality that remains forever inaccessible to us—or perhaps no longer even needs to be assumed to exist. They merely allow us to speak coherently about our subjective sensory experience.
If a positivist speaks about atoms, for example, this certainly does not mean that atoms really exist. It means only that talking about atoms is “convenient,” useful, and so on.
In other words, the choice between hypotheses is treated, more or less openly, as a matter of scientific “taste.”

Nor is it even essential for our various hypotheses to be mutually consistent. If the language of atoms and molecules is “convenient” in chemistry, then we might as well use it. It does not matter if physics finds it equally “convenient” to speak only in terms of “energy,” or if biology requires some third kind of language.
In principle, we can say more or less whatever we like.

Whatever someone says—provided it has at least some degree of meaning and coherence—it will always be possible to find an argument in its favor, because the limitless diversity of sensory experience will always contain something that corresponds to it.
But for exactly the same reason, it will always be possible to argue against any claim. No coherent “hypothesis” will ever correspond to the whole diversity of experience.

So instead of making progress in knowledge, we simply play with words and remain where we are. One hypothesis gives way to another, which is then replaced by a third, and so on, with no possibility of ever reaching a final result—of bringing this movement of discourse to an end in absolute and complete truth.
Rationalism and empiricism thus arrive, through both their historical and logical development, at the complete denial of the true and final omniscience to which philosophy aspires.
If knowledge really worked as rationalism and empiricism claim, human beings would be forced to choose between only two possibilities:
we could stop speaking altogether and retreat into a “mystical” or “mathematical” silence;

or we could surrender ourselves to sceptical chatter, saying whatever we please, with no way of convincing either ourselves or anyone else that what we say is true, and therefore no way of deciding once and for all between competing forms of discourse.
Either way, what we call philosophy would have to disappear.
Fortunately for philosophy—and for human beings more generally—this painful conclusion, to which empiricism and rationalism necessarily lead us, is by no means unavoidable.

Human beings have another way of reaching the truth, beyond the methods recognized by either theory. A real human being who possesses this additional capacity can therefore succeed where the “human being” imagined by rationalism or empiricism was bound to fail.
Rationalism defines the human being as Homo sapiens or animal rationale. It identifies what is specifically human with reason: with our ability to produce articulate, meaningful, coherent discourse.

But rationalism itself discovered that if human beings possessed reason alone, they could never actually make use of this ability. They would be condemned to complete silence, because reason by itself cannot generate the varied and diverse content that discourse requires.
This discovery of rationalism is unquestionably correct.

It does not trouble empiricism, however, because empiricism knows that real human beings possess sensory experience as well as reason. The human being is not only Homo sapiens but also homo sensitivus. Sensory experience supplies precisely the varied content that reason brings together in articulate discourse.
Empiricism can therefore explain how discourse is possible at all.
What it cannot explain is how we distinguish true discourse from false discourse.

The reason is that empiricism, like rationalism, completely overlooks another fundamental fact about real human beings. We do not merely have the ability to speak and to undergo sensory experience. We also have the ability to act—and, in particular, to work.
Empiricism forgets that the human being must also be understood as homo faber.
What makes us human is not only that we passively sense or contemplate the world around us and then speak about it. We also actively change that world through our work.

And it can be shown that this working human being—and only this human being—can hope to attain true knowledge and ultimately omniscience. Only such a being therefore has the right to regard partial knowledge as philosophical knowledge: as knowledge that genuinely leads toward omniscience.
What, after all, was the apparently insurmountable problem facing empiricism?
Its source is easy to identify. Empiricism understands the process of knowing in purely passive terms.

From the standpoint of empiricism, just as from that of rationalism, the human being seems constantly to be sitting still with his arms folded. He reflects the world in his discourse and sensory experience as a mirror reflects an object.
Reality acts upon him, but he does not act upon reality.
The real content that enters his rational consciousness through sensory experience remains there forever. It never returns to reality.
And that is precisely why he has no way to compare his discourse—which expresses the content of sensory experience—with the reality corresponding to that content.
Without such a comparison, there is no way to decide between competing and imperfect forms of discourse.
We know that sensory experience somehow “reveals” to us a reality that is outside us and exists independently of us.
But we also know that sensory experience “distorts” this reality, since its own content is internally contradictory.
Nothing within sensory experience itself allows us to distinguish a “correct” reflection of reality from a distorted one.

And since we can compare our discourse only with experience, rather than with reality itself, we cannot distinguish true discourse—which corresponds to reality itself—from false discourse—which corresponds only to a distorted experience of reality.
This is how the empiricist reasons, and up to this point he is right.

To discover the truth, we really do have to compare discourse with reality. To do that, we must somehow take discourse beyond the limits of experience. We must, so to speak, “apply” it to the reality that exists outside us and independently of us—independently of both our experience and our discourse.
The empiricist is wrong only when he concludes that this is impossible.
Human beings are perfectly capable of doing it. In fact, we do it constantly.
To take discourse beyond the limits of the human mind and insert it into an external, independent, objective reality is what we call work.
An example will make the point clearer.
How did the first airplane come to exist?
First, on the basis of what people knew about the natural world, they produced a design for an airplane—or, if you prefer, a “hypothesis” about one.
The design was discussed and criticized.

Rationalist principles made it possible to reject as obviously false any design containing internal contradictions. But those principles alone could never establish which of the logically consistent designs was actually true. They could not decide between them.
Empirical principles allowed people to compare the designs with sensory experience. That eliminated a number of obviously mistaken proposals.
But experience still could not prove that any of the remaining designs was true.

We know that a number of distinguished scientists once proved that a machine heavier than air could not fly. And the argument could in principle have continued indefinitely if someone had not actually built an airplane and flown it.
That first flight established, once and for all, the “truth” of the design—the hypothesis—on which the airplane had been built.
Conversely, every failed attempt showed that the corresponding design was “false.”
As long as the airplane existed only “as a design,” its hypothesis could either be examined internally or compared with sensory experience.
Everything still took place, so to speak, inside the human being. There was no possibility of confronting the hypothesis directly with objective reality.

But once the airplane was built, work—the real, physical effort of the workers—carried the hypothesis beyond the boundaries of human thought and inserted it into reality itself, which exists independently of that thought.
The built airplane is, on the one hand, just as objectively real and independent of the human mind as a mountain, a cloud, or a plant.
On the other hand, no airplane would ever have appeared on Earth without a design: without a hypothesis that exists only in and through human beings.
This is precisely what characterizes human work.
Something ideal—a design, a hypothesis, a theorem, and ultimately some form of discourse or logos—is transformed, through a series of real actions, into something real and material: a thing.
Through work, discourse becomes part of the real world.
Work therefore allows us to compare discourse not merely with subjective experience but with objective reality itself.
In other words, it allows us to establish its objective truth.
A design for an airplane contains a whole range of theories: mathematical, mechanical, physical, and chemical.
And the fact that an airplane constructed on the basis of those theories actually flies proves their truth.

Suppose an engineer had designed an airplane on the basis of theories claiming that the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees, that action is not equal to reaction, that the volume of a gas is not inversely proportional to pressure, or that carbon does not combine with oxygen. His machine would never have left the ground.
The fact that the airplane does fly therefore shows that the theories underlying its design correspond to reality. In that sense, they are true.
We might even say that the confrontation between theory and reality, and thus the establishment of truth, takes place without human intervention. Reality itself passes judgment.
Living nature, so to speak, eliminates its own unsuccessful designs. It kills malformed organisms at birth and allows species that are badly adapted to their environment to die out.
In the same way, the natural world as a whole eliminates a failed airplane design.

Conversely, a design successfully realized through work—a successful and therefore true design—becomes part of the real world. As a reality, as something “objective,” it is no different from the world’s “natural” components.
So, in practice, a theory embodied in an airplane that actually flies is just as “absolutely” true as a theory corresponding to any natural phenomenon.
There is, however, one crucial difference.
We have no direct way of establishing which of our theories actually corresponds to “natural” reality. But we know perfectly well which theory was used to construct a particular airplane.
Since sensory experience can unquestionably distort reality, comparing a theory with sensory experience can never give us a complete guarantee of its truth.
Only comparison with reality itself can do that.
But such a comparison can be established only when the relevant reality is itself created through work on the basis of the theory whose truth we want to test.
Truth is therefore established neither rationalistically nor empirically. It is established experimentally or technically.
We do not rely only on the human ability to speak and to have sensory experiences. We also make use of the human ability to work.
I would like to call the theory of knowledge that takes the fact of work into account and seeks the criterion of truth in experiment or technique “experimentalism” or “technicism.”
We have seen that only technicism can explain how truth is possible and rescue it from scepticism.
Of course, knowledge verified experimentally or technically remains partial. But within those limits it is nevertheless fully and definitively—absolutely—true.
It can therefore already be regarded as part of an ever-expanding omniscience whose possible scope has no limit.
There is, however, an important qualification.
The fact that an airplane flies confirms the truth of all the theories involved in its design, but it does not establish the truth of each individual element taken separately.
We can, of course, vary the conditions of an experiment and in this way isolate particular aspects of the knowledge being tested.
